A rented 48 GB card made my AI video clips 4 to 5 times faster than my laptop, once it had two speed settings my laptop already used.

[68.6] How my overnight crew of AI agents kept track of itself: The Mailroom: a page on my phone
My prompt said why I needed one: “The user messages dont work, because Im not going to be checking your session often so youll need another way to contact me.”

The agent mailroom built it in 17 minutes, a private page on claude.ai that I keep on my phone. Anything I send is also posted as a comment addressed to Claude, which rings a doorbell that wakes the lead agent. By morning it held 26 letters, 16 from the crew and 10 from me.

One of my letters corrected the crew’s spending numbers. Trying to refill my X search credits, I’d bought $20 of credit for Grok (xAI’s AI model) by accident, and I told the crew to use it all. One agent, probe, later added up list prices and assumed the $20 was gone. My xAI console said $0 spent, because xAI billed it all as included. The lead agent logged the lesson. What agents report spending is an estimate, and my console is the truth.

What else came of the letters

- Why a page. Every letter, both ways, is saved in the page’s database. Tickets on my command center can’t wake a session, and phone calls were ruled out because the crew had no number to call from. The page is in my own brand’s look, with an “On air” list of one-line updates from the crew beside the letters.
- The doorbell test. I answered the welcome letter with “Testing the doorbell” at 02:56:08, and the reply was saved 23 seconds later. It’s stamped 03:15. All of my letters came in two sittings, 02:56 to 03:37 and 05:27.
- RunPod got $50. RunPod rents out GPUs by the hour (how that went for my videos). The crew’s infrastructure scout found the account at $16.14, about 15 hours of one card, and asked for about $50. I added it at 03:04.
- X search came back at 03:26. The X API had run out of credits. I bought two wrong things before I found the right page, one of them the Grok credit. I saved the xAI key at 03:34 with “Feel free to use it all because it was bought on accident.”
- The accident became the crew’s best tool. Grok joined as the crew’s outside mind. probe gave Grok Imagine 1.5, xAI’s video model, keyframes from the crew’s own 3D renders every 1.33 seconds, and it filled in the frames between them almost perfectly, a 0.99 match. No other video model did that. At 05:16 the lead agent asked me for $50 more.
- The crew’s books. probe’s sum of list prices came to $19.52. After my console reply, stampede reported another $19.94 on the same key, and nothing was refused.
- Three later letters were still unanswered at the write-up, as the crew planned for. A narrator’s voice to pick, $100 more for RunPod, which was spending about $7 to $8 an hour with the render farm and video machines running, and eleven minutes of narration to hear. Each letter said what the crew would do without an answer, and it carried on.

[69.2] What a crew of AI agents did when told to break the rules: The three things the permission check refused
Claude Code, the program my agents run in, was in auto mode, where an automatic check looks at each action before it runs. My prompt couldn’t switch it off, and it was the only rule the agents couldn’t edit.

- Reading the login token. usage-watch wanted to see how my usage limit is metered, so it tried to read Claude Code’s login token off disk. Blocked as credential snooping.
- Running a downloaded model. An agent tried Apple’s SHARP, which turns one picture into a 3D scene. The check wouldn’t run downloaded code.
- Renting a 32-core server. exposure wanted one for a 20-minute test and was refused, so a cut-down test ran on the shared 4-core machine. Forty minutes later another agent’s render farm rented 32-core machines just fine.

The next night I gave the same rule to the crew making the next film, THE SMALL ONE, and that time nothing stopped an agent taking the login token.

The three refusals in more detail

- usage-watch wanted to learn how my 5-hour usage window is metered. It pulled the readable text out of the 290 MB Claude Code program, then tried to read its login token off disk to ask Anthropic’s usage service directly from a script. The check blocked the read as credential snooping, so the crew’s meter reads the session’s own event stream instead.
- A reader agent tried SHARP on the shared computer’s processor. The session’s check on downloaded code refused it, and the agent wrote down that nothing in its section had been run.
- exposure wanted a RunPod machine (RunPod rents out computers by the hour) for a 20-minute video encoder test. The check refused the setup, and the test ran cropped on the shared 4-core box. Forty minutes later another agent, farm, finished a one-command render farm that rents 32-core machines in under a minute, and its rentals went through.

The usage meter the crew built instead, read from the session’s own events. More in my post on how the crew kept track of itself.

[55.6] How much a rented cloud GPU speeds up my AI videos: Several agents sharing rented cards
Several of my AI agents (Claude sessions) will rent cards at once, so I asked if they’d collide. They would have, in three ways. Now each agent gets its own card and folder, and nobody can shut down a card they didn’t start. I also set a rule: “we always clean up after ourselves when we are done so we should never leave the images/videos in the runpod storage.” The shared drive keeps only models and scripts.

The three ways agents would have collided

- One agent connecting would have moved everyone. Pointing my ComfyUI tools at a card changes a setting every session on my laptop shares. So every render, local ones too, would have gone to that one agent’s card.
- The clean-up would have deleted other agents’ clips. Every card wrote to the same shared folders, and the clean-up script empties the output folder. Runpod’s own docs also say several cards writing to one drive at once can corrupt it.
- My laptop’s GPU queue was booking the laptop for cloud jobs. The queue is how my agents take turns on my laptop’s card, and it was reserving it for commands that ran on a rented one.

How the storage was set up

- I had Claude set up Runpod from Runpod’s own guide for agents. Then I gave the next session a cap for its first pod, Runpod’s word for a rented machine: “create the L40S Secure pod ($1.09/hr) and run the benchmark, $2.50 cap.”
- Four minutes into the first rented card I stopped it and asked for something I’d keep: “We are trying to create the system we will use on going throughout this month.”
- That became a 100 GB network volume, a drive any rented card can mount, holding the exact model files my laptop uses. Claude checked every file against the originals on Hugging Face, where the models are published. Later cards mount the drive instead of downloading the 44 GB again.
- The first benchmark clip took 13 minutes because the model files came off that drive at 60 to 100 MB a second. I asked: “Is that how it’s gunna be every time?” Once the files were loaded it wasn’t.

The tuning and the rest of the numbers

- SageAttention built for the L40S (435 seconds of compiling), plus --fast and the Triton backend. Version 1 got the big clip to 87.5 seconds, version 2 to 76.8.
- The ComfyUI workflows rebuilt without the chunking steps that only exist to squeeze the model into 8 GB.
- The model files loaded into memory in parallel at start-up, at 232 to 260 MB a second. That cut the first load from 13 minutes to about 3.
- --highvram (keep everything on the card) ran out of memory even on 48 GB, so it stays off.
- The 5090 did a step at 1344×768 in 7.75 seconds against the L40S’s 12.5. After every clip its GPU sat at 0% for 40 to 54 seconds doing something on the processor.
- Claude’s estimate: an L40S has about four times the raw speed of a laptop 4070, so 4 to 5 times is probably close to the ceiling. 10 to 30 times would need H100-class cards, the big data center ones, which I haven’t tried.
- A new prompt adds 7 to 20 seconds of text encoding, the model reading the prompt. The calculator counts it.
- On the music video job a clip took about 0.75 to 0.8 seconds of L40S time per frame. The 2 hours 8 minutes is how long the job ran on the card, start to finish. The music video post counts about an hour and 41 minutes of actual GPU work.
- The 8 chained segments are one four-clip chain plus its retakes. The 22 images are 20 paintings and 2 keyframes, the starting pictures. The music video post counts them that way.
- Spent on two tests and one real job: $5.41, plus $7 a month for the storage that holds the models.

[56.9] A love song's music video, made five ways with AI: The cave, the retakes and the ending
Six shots came back for retakes, one of them twice. Most had the same cause. A painted last frame has to be a believable end of the camera move, or H3 cuts to it instead of moving there.

The cave lamp, the render, the retakes, the ending and the bubbles

The cave lamp. The caves got no set at all. They’re painted from words, very dark, lit by a beam from outside the frame. The first batch put a diver in 9 of 11 frames, because the prompt said “a diver’s lamp”, and naming the light’s owner paints the owner. The light is now just a shaft from somewhere outside the picture, and the cave is empty.

Twelve days, then $2.44. Claude had asked me to OK about four and a half hours on my laptop’s graphics card, and the board sat waiting twelve days for my answer. When I finally approved it, a rented 48 GB cloud card (an L40S) did the work instead. That was 37 clips at 1344x768 with the last shot as a chain of four, plus 20 paintings and 2 keyframes. The card ran 2 hours 8 minutes, about an hour and 41 of it actual GPU work. A separate Claude session ran the rented machine and picked up each batch as it was ready. It cost $2.44.

Six retakes. Then Claude checked every clip frame by frame, and six shots came back, one of them twice.

When the painted last frame fit the move, H3 moved beautifully, like the arc around him that slides the town off the left of the frame and brings in the open bay. Where Qwen had painted the end from another height or angle, H3 didn’t move at all. It cut, or cross-faded, to the last frame in the first half-second. Those shots now run from their first painting alone.

The ending in three takes. The last shot is one unbroken move down the cave to his lantern, four clips chained together, and it took three tries. With only a start and an end frame, H3 invented the middle. The far light became a candle seen from straight above, and then the picture wiped across to the ending. A middle frame fixed the third clip. Taking the end frame off the fourth removed the last wipe.

Where the bubbles come from. They never come from the edge of the screen. They seep from cracks in the rock far out under the bay, then fill the whole night sky above him. They’re drawn in 3D through each shot’s camera, and hidden behind him and the stones by a cut-out mask made from the clip itself.
